title: Fat and Thin
text:
On a platform of the Nikolaevsky railway station two old school friends ran into each other. One was fat, freshly dined, smelling of sherry and orange blossom. The other was thin, loaded with bags and parcels, accompanied by his thin wife and his lanky son.

They embraced three times and stood with tears in their eyes. The thin man talked happily about their school days, introduced his family and told how life had gone. He was a collegiate assessor now, a modest civil service rank, and his wife gave music lessons. "And you, my dear friend, how far have you got?"

"I am a privy councillor," said the fat man. "I have two stars."

The thin man turned pale and went stiff. His face twisted into a broad, sugary smile. He seemed to shrink, and so did his bags and his family. "Your Excellency, I am very pleased," he stammered. "A friend, one might say, of my childhood, and now risen to such a height." His wife smiled, his son clicked his heels and dropped his cap.

"Come, come," the fat man said, frowning. "What is this tone? We were boys together. There is no need for this rank business." But the thin man only giggled and cringed further. The fat man felt sick. He turned away, gave the thin man his hand to say goodbye, and left.
lesson: Respect for rank can destroy real connection. Treat people the same whatever their title, and do not shrink yourself in front of status.
people: Two old school friends, the thin man's wife and son
source: Anton Chekhov, Fat and Thin (Tolstyi i tonkii, 1883)
